analogy.p: Imagine posting a long book to a friend one page at a time. You number each page, put each in an envelope with your friend's address, and the post office sends every envelope by whichever lorry route is quickest. The envelopes arrive in a jumble, so your friend sorts them by page number and phones you to ask for any that are missing. The numbering is TCP, the address on the envelope is IP, the sorting offices are routers, and the whole system of agreed rules is the protocol. It breaks down because real post offices do not usually ask for lost pages to be resent automatically, and data packets travel at almost the speed of light.
analogy.t: The postal service sending a book

bullets: A protocol is a set of **rules** for communication between devices; a **standard** is an agreed, published version of those rules.
Standards give **compatibility**: any browser can load a page from any web server because both follow HTTP.
Protocols cover things such as data format, addressing, error checking, speed of transmission, and how to start and stop a connection.
The protocols on the J277 specification are **TCP/IP, HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP and IMAP** (plus the link technologies Ethernet, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth).
Most protocols work together: loading one web page uses HTTP or HTTPS, TCP and IP at the same time, each doing a different job.
Exam link: a 1 mark answer to 'what is a protocol?' is 'a set of rules for how devices communicate / transfer data'.
core.h: What a protocol is, and why standards matter
core.p: A **protocol** is an agreed set of rules that decides how devices communicate: the format of the data, the order of messages, how errors are spotted and how a conversation starts and ends. Without agreed rules a laptop made by one company could not talk to a router made by another or to a web server on the other side of the world. OCR J277 1.3 expects you to know what each of the listed protocols is for, and to pick the right one for a scenario. Each protocol is a **standard**, meaning it is publicly agreed so that hardware and software from any manufacturer works together.

bullets: A **packet** is a small unit of data sent across a network.

Each packet has a **header** (typically the source and destination IP addresses and the packet number), a **payload** (the slice of the actual data) and **error-checking** information (often called the trailer).
The **packet number** lets the receiving device put the pieces back in the correct order, because packets can arrive out of order.
The **destination address** lets routers know where to send the packet next.
The **error check** lets the receiver spot a packet that was damaged in transit so that it can be requested again.
Example: a 3 MB file sent in packets carrying 1500 bytes of data each needs 3 000 000 ÷ 1500 = 2000 packets.
core.p: On a network, large pieces of data such as a photo or an email are not sent as one block. They are broken into small chunks called **packets**. Each packet is sent separately and the pieces are put back together at the destination. Sending small packets makes better use of the network, because many users' packets can share the same cables, and if one packet is damaged only that small piece has to be sent again instead of the whole file.

bullets: Step 1: the message is **split into packets** and each is given a packet number and the destination address.
Step 2: each packet is sent to the nearest **router**.
Step 3: each router reads the destination address and forwards the packet along the best available route; the packets of one message can take **different routes**.
Step 4: the packets arrive at the destination, possibly **out of order**.
Step 5: the destination uses the packet numbers to **reassemble** the message in the right order; any missing packet is requested again.
Advantages: efficient use of the network, a failed or busy route can be avoided, no dedicated line is needed, and many users share the same links.
Disadvantages: packets can arrive out of order or be delayed, so extra work is needed to reassemble them.
core.p: **Packet switching** is the method the internet uses to move packets. The message is split into packets, and each packet is passed from **router** to router towards its destination. At every router the destination address in the packet is read and the router decides the best next step at that moment. Because conditions change (a link may be busy or broken), different packets from the same message may take different routes, and they may arrive in a different order from the one they were sent in. The receiving device uses the packet numbers to reassemble them.

bullets: **TCP** = Transmission Control Protocol: splits data into packets, numbers them, checks for errors and lost packets, and reassembles the data in order.
TCP uses **acknowledgements**: the receiver confirms packets it has received, and the sender resends anything not acknowledged.
**IP** = Internet Protocol: adds the **source and destination IP addresses** and is responsible for routing packets across networks.
An **IP address** identifies a device on a network (for example 192.168.1.20) and works like a postal address.
Together they give reliable end-to-end delivery across many different networks.
Memory trick: **T**CP **T**ransports reliably; **I**P gives the **I**dentity (address) and route.
core.h: TCP/IP: two protocols that work as a pair
core.p: **TCP/IP** is the name for the family of rules that run the internet, and it is mainly made of two protocols. **TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol) looks after the conversation between two devices: it splits the data into packets, numbers them, checks they all arrive, asks for any missing packet again and reassembles the data at the other end. **IP** (Internet Protocol) looks after addressing and routing: it puts the source and destination **IP address** on each packet and lets routers forward it. TCP makes the transfer reliable; IP gets each packet to the right place.

bullets: **HTTP** = HyperText Transfer Protocol; used to request and send **web pages** between a browser (client) and a web server.
The browser sends a **request**; the web server sends a **response** containing the page.
Web pages are written in **HTML**, which the browser interprets to display the page.
Data is **not encrypted** in HTTP, so it can be read if intercepted.
It is fine for pages with no private information, but unsuitable for passwords or card details.
A web address (URL) beginning http:// uses HTTP.
core.p: **HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the protocol a web browser uses to ask a web server for a web page, and that the server uses to reply. The browser sends a request for a page; the web server sends back the page, usually written in HTML, which the browser then displays. Ordinary HTTP sends everything as plain readable text, so anyone able to intercept the packets could read it.

bullets: **HTTPS** = HTTP **S**ecure: web page transfer where the data is **encrypted**.
Uses **TLS** (Transport Layer Security), the successor to **SSL**, to encrypt the connection.
The website holds a **digital certificate** that helps the browser check that the site is genuine.
Browsers usually show a **padlock** and the address begins https://.
It protects against **interception**: even if packets are captured, the encrypted data cannot be understood.
Use it wherever **passwords, card numbers or personal data** are sent.
It does not make a website trustworthy; a fake website can also use HTTPS, so users must still check the address.
core.p: **HTTPS** (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) is HTTP with **encryption** added. Before any data is exchanged, the browser and the website agree a secure connection using TLS (an updated version of SSL), and the website proves its identity with a **digital certificate**. After that, everything sent is encrypted, so intercepted packets are unreadable without the key. This is why online banking and shopping sites must use HTTPS.

bullets: **FTP** = File Transfer Protocol; used to **upload and download files** between a client and a server.
Typical uses: publishing website files, sharing large files with a company, and downloading software.
The user usually logs in with a **username and password**.
Basic FTP does **not encrypt** data, so secure alternatives (such as SFTP or FTPS) are used when files are confidential.
An FTP **client** is the program on the user's device; the FTP **server** stores the files.
Do not confuse it with HTTP: HTTP is for **web pages**, FTP is for **files**.
core.p: **FTP** (File Transfer Protocol) is used to transfer files between computers over a network. It is designed for moving files, such as uploading a finished website to a web hosting server or downloading a large file from a company server. A user runs an FTP client, connects to an FTP server (often with a username and password), and then uploads or downloads files. FTP is particularly useful for large files or many files at once.

bullets: **SMTP** = Simple Mail Transfer Protocol; used to **send** email from a client to a mail server and **between** mail servers.
It pushes email towards the destination server.
It is **not** used for collecting email from a mailbox; that is POP or IMAP.
Exam rule: if the question says 'sending', answer **SMTP**; if it says 'receiving/retrieving/downloading', answer **POP or IMAP**.
A mail server stores each user's mailbox until they collect it.
core.p: **SMTP** (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is used to **send** email. When you press send, your email program uses SMTP to pass the message to your outgoing mail server. That server then uses SMTP again to pass it on towards the recipient's mail server, perhaps through several servers on the way. SMTP only handles sending and forwarding; it is not used to read your emails.

bullets: **POP** = Post Office Protocol; used to **download** email from the mail server to a device.
Emails are normally **deleted from the server** after they are downloaded.
Emails can be read **offline** once downloaded.
Emails are stored on **one device**, so they are not available on your other devices.
Frees up space on the server, but if the device fails the emails may be lost unless backed up.
POP is a **receiving** protocol, not for sending.
core.h: POP: collecting email by downloading it
core.p: **POP** (Post Office Protocol, commonly POP3) is used to **retrieve** email from a mail server. With POP, the messages are downloaded to the device you are using and are normally then removed from the server. This means you can read them without an internet connection, but the emails now exist only on that one device, so another phone or computer will not see them.

bullets: **IMAP** = Internet Message Access Protocol; used to **view and manage** email stored on the server.
Emails **stay on the server**; devices show a synchronised view.
Works well with **multiple devices**: reading or deleting an email on a phone updates the laptop.
Emails are backed up on the server, so losing one device does not lose them.
Needs an internet connection to see full messages unless the email app caches them.
Uses server storage space, so mailboxes may have size limits.
core.h: IMAP: collecting email while leaving it on the server
core.p: **IMAP** (Internet Message Access Protocol) also retrieves email, but the emails are **kept on the mail server** and your device shows you what is on the server. Because every device views the same mailbox, anything you do, such as reading a message, deleting it or moving it to a folder, is **synchronised** everywhere. IMAP is therefore better when you check email on several devices.

bullets: POP: downloads, then (usually) **deletes from the server**; IMAP: **leaves** the email on the server.
POP: emails readable **offline**; IMAP: usually needs a connection to the server.
POP: emails on **one device**; IMAP: the **same inbox on all devices**.
POP: low server storage needed; IMAP: server storage is used.
Choose **IMAP** for a person using a phone, tablet and laptop; choose **POP** for one computer and a limited server mailbox.
Both are for **receiving**; neither sends email.
core.h: POP versus IMAP: comparison for the exam
core.p: A favourite exam question is to compare POP and IMAP, or to decide which one suits a person. The key idea is where the emails live. With POP they are moved to one device, and with IMAP they stay on the server and are shared by all devices. Always name the protocol and then state the consequence, because the mark is usually for the consequence.

bullets: **Ethernet**: standard for **wired** LANs, using copper or fibre-optic cables.
**Wi-Fi**: standard for **wireless** LANs, using radio waves, with a typical range of tens of metres.
**Bluetooth**: **short-range** wireless (a few metres) for headphones, keyboards and speakers.
These standards decide how bits are sent over the medium (the **link** between neighbouring devices).
They are lower-level than HTTP or TCP/IP; they get the packets across one hop of the journey.
Link to the four-layer model: Ethernet and Wi-Fi sit in the **link layer**.
core.h: Ethernet, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth as standards
core.p: Wired and wireless connections are also covered by protocols and standards. **Ethernet** is the standard for wired local area networks, **Wi-Fi** is the standard for wireless local area networks using radio waves, and **Bluetooth** is a short-range wireless standard for connecting nearby devices. They describe how the physical connection works, while TCP/IP, HTTP and the others operate above them.

bullets: The browser sends an **HTTP/HTTPS request** for the page.
**TCP** splits the data into numbered packets and manages reliable delivery.
**IP** adds source and destination **IP addresses**.
**Routers** forward the packets by **packet switching**.
**Ethernet/Wi-Fi** carries the signal across each local link.
The web server's reply returns by the same process and the browser displays the HTML page.
core.h: Putting it together: loading a web page
core.p: When you type a web address, several protocols cooperate. The browser asks for the page using HTTP or HTTPS. TCP splits the request and the response into numbered packets and checks they all arrive. IP puts addresses on the packets so routers can forward them, and Ethernet or Wi-Fi carries the packets across each local connection. At the other end the server's TCP reassembles the request and the server sends the page back the same way.

bullets: View ordinary web pages: **HTTP**.
Enter card details or log in to a bank: **HTTPS**, because the data is encrypted.
Upload a website or transfer a large file to a server: **FTP**.
Send an email: **SMTP**.
Collect email onto one device and read offline: **POP**.
Check the same mailbox from several devices: **IMAP**.
Send data reliably in packets and reassemble it: **TCP**; give each packet an address and route it: **IP**.
core.h: Choosing the right protocol for a scenario
core.p: Scenario questions give a situation and ask which protocol to use and why. The method is to underline the action in the question (view page, send email, collect email, transfer file, secure payment) and match it to the protocol. Then add a reason that links to the scenario, because bare protocol names often gain only one mark.

bullets: Security link: **HTTPS** and encryption reduce the risk of **interception**; plain HTTP and basic FTP do not.
Layers link: **HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP, IMAP** are application-layer protocols; **TCP** is the transport layer; **IP** is the internet layer.
Performance link: more traffic and congestion means more delay; packet switching helps by rerouting.
Reliability link: TCP **acknowledgements** and error checks mean lost packets are resent.
Cause-and-effect phrases earn marks: 'so that', 'because', 'which means'.
core.h: Links to other topics and Higher-level thinking
core.p: Protocols link directly to network security (HTTPS and encryption protect against interception), to the four-layer TCP/IP model (each protocol sits in a layer), and to network performance (packet switching and error checking affect speed and reliability). Strong answers show cause and effect, such as 'because packets can arrive out of order, TCP uses packet numbers to reassemble them'.

exam: 'State' or 'give' questions (1 mark) just need the name or purpose, e.g. 'SMTP is used to send email'.

Spell out abbreviations if asked: HTTP = HyperText Transfer Protocol, FTP = File Transfer Protocol, SMTP = Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, IMAP = Internet Message Access Protocol, POP = Post Office Protocol.

'Describe packet switching' (4 marks): split into packets; each has a header with destination address and packet number; routers send each packet by the best route, so packets may take different routes; reassembled in order at the destination.
'Explain' questions need a reason: 'HTTPS is used because the data is encrypted, so it cannot be read if intercepted'.
For POP v IMAP comparisons, write one point about each in the same row (where the email is stored, number of devices, offline access).
In scenario questions quote details from the question (e.g. 'she uses a phone and a laptop') and link them to IMAP.
Do not confuse sending (SMTP) with receiving (POP/IMAP); examiners often test this.
For 6 mark questions, structure the answer: what each protocol does, how they work together, then a conclusion about the scenario.
Never say packets 'always take the same route' or 'arrive in order'.
Use correct terms: **packet, header, router, destination address, encrypted, reassemble**.

mistakes.r: HTTPS is HTTP with encryption, so data cannot be read if intercepted.
mistakes.w: HTTP and HTTPS are 'the same thing'.

mistakes.r: SMTP is for sending (and forwarding) email; POP or IMAP is used to receive it.
mistakes.w: SMTP is used to receive emails.

mistakes.r: FTP transfers files; web pages are transferred using HTTP/HTTPS.
mistakes.w: FTP is used to view web pages.

mistakes.r: Packets can take different routes and arrive out of order; packet numbers are used to reassemble them.
TCP and IP are two protocols with different jobs: TCP manages delivery, IP does addressing and routing.
That describes POP. IMAP keeps the email on the server and synchronises devices.
mistakes.w: IMAP downloads the email and deletes it from the server.

mistakes.r: The padlock only means the connection is encrypted (HTTPS); the site could still be fake.
mistakes.w: A padlock means the website is safe or trustworthy.

mistakes.r: Name the protocol and add a reason linked to the scenario (e.g. HTTPS because card details must be encrypted).
mistakes.w: Just writing the protocol name in a scenario question.

summary: OCR J277 1.3 asks you to know the purpose of the main network protocols (TCP/IP, HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP and IMAP), how data is sent as packets using packet switching, and to choose the right protocol for a scenario. It matters because Paper 1 regularly asks you to name a protocol, explain what it does and justify a choice.

terms.d: A set of rules that allows devices to communicate and transfer data.
An agreed set of rules or specifications that allows hardware and software from different manufacturers to work together.
A small unit of data sent across a network, containing a header, the payload (data) and error-checking information.
The part of a packet holding information such as source address, destination address and packet number.
The part of a packet that carries the actual data being sent.
A method of data transmission in which a message is split into packets, each of which may take a different route to the destination and be reassembled there.
A device that forwards packets between networks using their destination addresses.
Transmission Control Protocol: splits data into packets, numbers them, checks for errors and reassembles them in order.
Internet Protocol: addresses packets and routes them across networks.
A number that identifies a device on a network.
HyperText Transfer Protocol: used to transfer web pages between a web server and a browser.
HTTP Secure: HTTP with the data encrypted.
Security protocols that encrypt data sent between a browser and a web server.
An electronic document that helps prove a website is genuine.
File Transfer Protocol: used to upload and download files to and from a server.
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: used to send email.
Post Office Protocol: downloads email from a server to a device, usually deleting the server copy.
Internet Message Access Protocol: lets you view and manage email that stays on the server.

worked.ans: The file is split into packets, each with a header containing the destination address and a packet number. Routers forward each packet along the best available route, so the packets may take different routes and arrive out of order. At the destination the packets are put back in order using the packet numbers and any missing packet is requested again.
worked.q: Describe how a large file is sent from one computer to another over the internet using packet switching. [4 marks]
steps: Mark 1: the file is split into small packets.
Mark 2: each packet has a header holding the destination address and a packet number.
Mark 3: routers read the destination address and pass each packet on by the best available route, so packets can take different routes.
Mark 4: the packets are reassembled in the correct order at the destination using the packet numbers (and any missing packet is requested again).

worked.ans: POP downloads email to a single device and normally removes it from the server, so the phone and tablet would not show messages downloaded to the laptop. IMAP leaves the email on the server and synchronises every device, so reading or deleting an email on one device is shown on all of them. IMAP is therefore the best choice for this user.
worked.q: Compare POP and IMAP for a person who reads email on a phone, a tablet and a laptop. Recommend one. [4 marks]
steps: POP downloads the emails to one device and usually deletes them from the server.
IMAP keeps the emails on the server and all devices see the same mailbox.
With three devices, the user needs the same inbox everywhere, so IMAP is better.

worked.q: A photo of size 3 MB is sent in packets. Each packet carries 1500 bytes of data. Calculate the number of packets needed. (Use 1 MB = 1 000 000 bytes.) [2 marks]
steps: Divide by the data per packet: 3 000 000 ÷ 1500.
